questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “move” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A knot is studied as a diagram: a closed loop drawn on paper with a mark at each crossing to show which strand passes over. Two diagrams stand for the same knot when one can be turned into the other by a sequence of three permitted alterations, which twist a loop, slide one strand across another, or lift a strand past a crossing. Anything done to a diagram outside that list changes the knot and not merely the picture, so every step of a proof is written as a <u>move</u> of one of the three kinds.

choices.label: A
choices.content: One of a fixed set of permitted alterations that leaves the knot itself unchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A calculated action taken in order to achieve an aim.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A player's turn in a game played on a board.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A change of position from one place to another.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A crystalline solid ground to a fine powder presents its planes of atoms in every orientation at once, and a beam of X-rays passed through it emerges as a set of concentric rings. The spacing of those rings and their relative strength depend on the arrangement of the atoms and on nothing else, so two samples of one compound give the same set whatever their history. A chemist matching an unknown against a catalogue of published patterns therefore treats the rings as _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Before 1910 the pine forests of the interior West burned lightly every ten or fifteen years, and the flames consumed the litter and the seedlings without reaching the crowns of the older trees. Eighty years of prompt suppression allowed both to accumulate, until the small trees formed a continuous ladder from the ground to the canopy. The fires that eventually arrive are not the fires that were stopped. Suppression did not remove the hazard; it _____ it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Four thousand years of selection have left the domesticated silkmoth unable to live outside a rearing house. The adult's wings are far too small to carry its body, the larvae will not crawl in search of food when a mulberry branch is taken away, and the pale colouring that makes a cocoon easy to sort would betray the insect to any bird. The moth is now wholly _____ the people who keep it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Rather more than half the neurons of an octopus lie in its eight arms and not in the brain between its eyes. An arm separated from the body will still recoil from an irritant and will still pass a piece of food along its suckers towards a mouth that is no longer there. In intact animals the brain appears to name a target and to leave the arm to find its own way to it. Control of the limbs is therefore _____.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A bottle described as corked has not oxidised and has not turned to vinegar. It carries a trace of trichloroanisole, a compound formed when moulds in the bark act on chlorinated residues left there by bleaching, and the human nose detects it at a few parts in a million million, well below the level at which any instrument in ordinary cellar use will report it. The fault lies in the closure and not in the wine, which is why a second bottle from the same case is very often sound.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To identify the cause of a particular fault in bottled wine and to place it in the closure rather than the wine.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To argue that screw caps ought to replace cork in the bottling of wine.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To describe the process by which cork bark is harvested and prepared for use.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To explain why some drinkers detect faint smells that others cannot.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A gannet enters the water from thirty metres up at something near a hundred kilometres an hour, and an impact of that kind would drive water into the skull of most birds. <u>The gannet has no external nostrils at all, and a network of air sacs lies between the skin of its breast and the muscle beneath, taking up the blow much as packing takes up the shock to a crate.</u> A bird may make several hundred such dives in a day's fishing and shows no injury from any of them.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It compares the gannet's diving speed with the speeds reached by other seabirds.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It concedes that the diving method carries a risk the bird cannot avoid.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It identifies the features that account for the outcome reported in the final sentence.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It explains how the bird judges the depth at which a fish is swimming.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Fire kills the visible part of a mallee eucalypt and leaves the plant alive. Beneath the soil sits a woody swelling formed in the seedling's first years and packed with dormant buds and stored starch, and the heat that removes the stems does not reach it. Within weeks of a fire the swelling sends up a dozen new shoots at once, drawing on reserves the burnt canopy had laid down. A stand that appears to have been destroyed may consist of individuals that were already old when the fire passed through it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Fire removes the canopy of a mallee eucalypt but leaves the surrounding ground unharmed.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The woody swelling of a mallee is formed during the first years of the seedling's life.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Stands of mallee recover from fire more quickly than other kinds of woodland do.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A mallee survives fire in a buried structure holding both buds and food, so a stand regrows from established plants rather than from seed.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A barometer tells an observer what the pressure is where he stands, and a falling glass gave a captain some warning of a storm already close. What no observer could obtain was the state of the atmosphere across a whole country at one moment, since a letter reporting yesterday's wind at a distant station arrived days after it could be of use. The electric telegraph removed the delay. From 1849 stations wired their readings to a central office, a clerk entered them on a blank map, and the shape of a storm could be seen for the first time.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Storms came to be understood by clerks in a central office rather than by observers in the field.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Nineteenth-century observers recorded atmospheric pressure more accurately than their predecessors had.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Weather could be mapped across a region only once reports were able to travel faster than the weather itself.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The barometer was of little use to sailors until the telegraph was invented.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Barreto's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
Acid inherited from the grape gives a white wine its freshness, and a grape loses acid as it ripens. Four blocks of one variety, all picked at the same sugar level, were compared over a single season. Oenologist Ines Barreto argues that the acid a grape keeps depends on how cool its nights are rather than on how much sun the block receives.
BlockMean night temperature during ripening (°C)Direct sun (hours per day)Acidity at harvest (g/L)
North ridge128.57.4
Valley floor198.45.1
Coastal terrace136.97.1
Inland slope187.05.3

choices.label: A
choices.content: The coastal terrace received 6.9 hours of direct sun a day and finished at 7.1 g/L.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The two blocks with the coolest nights, the north ridge at 12 °C and the coastal terrace at 13 °C, finished at 7.4 and 7.1 g/L, while the valley floor and the inland slope, at 19 °C and 18 °C, finished at 5.1 and 5.3 g/L, even though those pairs do not divide by hours of sun.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The north ridge received 8.5 hours of direct sun a day, more than any other block, and finished at 7.4 g/L.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The valley floor recorded the warmest nights, at 19 °C, and the lowest acidity at harvest, 5.1 g/L.

questions.stem: Which quotation from the diary most effectively illustrates Bercovitch's claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A collector who spent four summers in the Hebrides between 1906 and 1910 kept a diary alongside her notebooks of tunes. Ethnomusicologist Jonah Bercovitch argues that the diary treats the singers as the authorities on their own repertoire rather than as sources whose performances required correction by the person writing them down.

choices.label: A
choices.content: “The singer's voice is low and carries little, and I sat close by the fire in order to hear the words at all.”

choices.label: B
choices.content: “Mrs MacAulay sang the second verse to a different close, and when I asked which was right she said both were, and that her mother had sung them so. I have set down the two and will not choose between them.”

choices.label: C
choices.content: “The weather kept us indoors for three days, and I copied out the tunes taken at Barra in a fair hand.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “Eleven songs taken this week, of which four are variants of tunes already in the notebook.”

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nkosi's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Seed of several South African shrubs lies in the soil for years and germinates in numbers only after a fire has passed over it. Two things a fire delivers might account for that: a brief pulse of heat through the top few centimetres of soil, and the smoke that soaks into the ground as it drifts. Botanist Thabo Nkosi argues that the cue is chemical rather than thermal.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Seed watered with smoke that had been bubbled through cold water germinated as freely as seed lifted from a burnt site, while seed heated in an oven to the temperatures a fire produces germinated no better than untreated seed.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Fires in the region are most frequent at the end of a dry summer.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The temperature a metre below the surface hardly changes while a fire passes overhead.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Seedlings appearing after a fire face less competition than seedlings appearing in unburnt vegetation.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An archive holds a wax cylinder recorded in a Somerset kitchen in 1907. The singer was seventy, sang a single verse because the cylinder would hold no more, and had learned the song from a carter who died before anyone thought to write anything down. Twenty other people in the same parish are known to have sung it. A scholar who treats the cylinder as the song rather than as one performance of it is therefore liable to _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: underestimate the age of the version the singer had learned.

choices.label: B
choices.content: attribute the song to the carter rather than to the singer.

choices.label: C
choices.content: overlook the technical limitations of early recording equipment.

choices.label: D
choices.content: mistake the features of a single occasion for properties of the song itself.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Roman law allowed a possessor to become owner after holding a thing for a fixed period, one year for movables and two for land. The rule closed disputes that no evidence could settle, but it was hedged about: the possession had to have begun in good faith, and the thing itself had to be capable of the benefit, a stolen object being permanently barred from it however long it was held and through however many hands it passed. A jurist advising a purchaser who had bought in complete innocence from a thief would therefore have said that the buyer _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: could acquire ownership only after the longer period fixed for land.

choices.label: B
choices.content: was liable to the same penalty as the thief who had sold it to him.

choices.label: C
choices.content: could never acquire ownership of the thing by holding it, whatever his own state of mind.

choices.label: D
choices.content: became owner of the thing after one year, since he had acquired it in good faith.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: The Bank of England's notes were payable in gold on demand through most of the nineteenth century, and the promise was kept. Two wars suspended that _____ note that circulates today is legal tender because Parliament says so, and not because anything is held against it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The bath in which a wet plate is sensitised holds silver nitrate in solution, and it grows weaker with every plate that passes through it. A photographer who has coated six plates in an afternoon and has begun to see thin, patchy _____ the strength of the bath before blaming the light.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Every large telescope built before 1890 used a lens, and a lens more than a metre across sags under its own weight. The reflector that replaced _____ whose mirror can be supported across the whole of its back, has no such limit.

questions.passage: A supercell is not merely a large thunderstorm. What sets it apart is a single updraught that rotates, and that rotation _____ the storm to stand clear of the rain it produces instead of being killed by its own downdraught within the hour.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Two diagrams of what may be the same knot rarely look alike, and the only way to be sure is to reach one from the other by permitted moves. Working through a long sequence of such moves on a diagram of eleven crossings, _____

choices.content: there was no steady fall in the number of crossings.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the number of crossings fell to seven and then rose again to nine.

choices.label: C
choices.content: a student in the seminar brought it down to seven crossings and then watched it rise again to nine.

choices.label: D
choices.content: it became clear that the count does not fall steadily.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: A property that survives every permitted redrawing of a diagram can be used to tell two knots apart, and a good deal of the subject consists of hunting for such properties. _____ the smallest number of crossings a knot can be drawn with does not change however the picture is rearranged, so a knot needing seven cannot be the same as one needing three.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how the heavy-metal soak supplies what the measurement leaves out. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A diffraction measurement records how strong each reflected beam is.
  • It records nothing about the phase of the wave that produced the beam.
  • Both quantities are needed in order to calculate where the atoms lie.
  • Soaking a crystal in a heavy-metal salt adds a few dense atoms at fixed sites.
  • The changes those atoms make to the recorded strengths allow the missing phases to be worked out.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Both the strength and the phase of each reflected beam are needed before the positions of the atoms can be calculated.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Since a measurement records the strength of each beam but not its phase, and both are needed to locate the atoms, the crystal is soaked in a heavy-metal salt whose few dense atoms alter the recorded strengths in ways from which the missing phases can be worked out.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A diffraction measurement records how strong each reflected beam is but nothing about its phase.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Soaking a crystal in a heavy-metal salt introduces a few dense atoms at fixed sites within it.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the 1976 proof was received differently from the proofs that had come before it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The four colour conjecture holds that any map can be coloured with four colours so that no two neighbouring regions share one.
  • It resisted proof for more than a century.
  • Appel and Haken reduced the problem in 1976 to about 1,500 unavoidable configurations.
  • Each of those configurations was checked by computer.
  • No mathematician has read the whole of the case-by-case checking.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Appel and Haken reduced a conjecture that had resisted proof for a century to about 1,500 configurations and checked each one by computer, so the argument was complete although no mathematician had read the case-by-case checking it rested on.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The four colour conjecture holds that any map can be coloured with four colours without two neighbouring regions sharing one.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Appel and Haken reduced the problem in 1976 to about 1,500 unavoidable configurations.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The four colour conjecture had resisted proof for more than a century before 1976.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the method depended on developments in glassmaking. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The second fermentation of a sparkling wine is carried out in the sealed bottle, not in a vat.
  • The carbon dioxide it produces cannot escape and dissolves in the wine.
  • The pressure in a finished bottle reaches about six atmospheres.
  • Early producers lost a large part of every cellar to bursting glass.
  • Coal-fired English furnaces made a stronger, darker glass than the wood-fired French ones.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Early producers of sparkling wine lost a large part of every cellar to bursting glass.

choices.label: B
choices.content: English glass furnaces burned coal and produced a stronger, darker glass than the wood-fired furnaces of France.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Since the second fermentation is finished inside a sealed bottle, the gas cannot escape and the bottle stands at about six atmospheres, a pressure that burst much of every early cellar and that only the stronger glass of coal-fired English furnaces could contain.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A second fermentation is carried out in the sealed bottle rather than in an open vat.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A collector who worked with a notebook wrote down what a singer sang in the staff notation he had been taught at school. That notation has no sign for a note sung a little below the third of the scale, none for a line ended by letting the voice fall away, and none for a beat held a fraction longer than the bar allows. Whatever he could not spell simply left the record. His transcriptions are therefore _____ rather than false.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A cart wheel is not a flat disc. Its spokes lean outward from the hub so that the rim stands in a shallow cone, and to anyone who has not built one the wheel looks as though it has already begun to collapse. The shape is in fact _____: a loaded cart rocks from side to side on rough ground, and the cone braces the wheel against the thrust that the rocking sends along the axle.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A larger mirror gathers more light, but that light has already crossed several miles of moving air, and the motion smears a star into a trembling disc. No further polishing of the glass improves matters. Committees that had once chosen a site by the convenience of the nearest railway began instead to send an assistant to camp on a ridge for a season with a small telescope, judging the steadiness of the air before any foundation was laid. The ground had come to seem no less _____ than the instrument.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A mint that put less silver into a penny while leaving its face value untouched kept the difference, and a treasury short of money found the temptation hard to resist. Merchants, however, weighed coin as readily as they counted it. Within a season of a debasement the old heavy pennies had gone into hoards or out of the country, prices quoted in the new money had risen to match its metal, and the crown's gain had proved _____.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “recruitment” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A colony's size in any season reflects two quantities that are counted separately. Adults that bred the year before return to the same ledges and are recorded as such. Birds hatched three or four seasons earlier arrive to breed for the first time, take a place at the edge of the colony and are entered under a different heading, since a colony losing adults faster than it gains these newcomers is in decline however many eggs it laid. Long runs of ringing data are kept chiefly in order to measure <u>recruitment</u>.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The enlistment of new members into an armed force.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The entry of young birds into the breeding population of a colony.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The hiring of staff to fill posts in an organisation.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A fresh supply of stores brought to a remote settlement.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: By the sixth century the writings of the classical jurists ran to something like two thousand volumes, many of them contradicting one another and some surviving only in quotation. Justinian appointed a commission to reduce the whole of it to one work. The compilers cut what had become obsolete, altered the wording where two opinions clashed, and arranged what remained by subject, attributing each extract to the jurist who wrote it. The Digest that resulted is a fiftieth of the bulk it was drawn from and reads as though the law had never been in dispute.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It compares Roman law with the legal systems that came after it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It describes a body of material and the difficulties it presented, then explains how a compilation altered it and what the result is like.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It traces the careers of the classical jurists whose writings were eventually compiled.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It argues that the compilers should have preserved the disagreements they removed.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: X-rays scattered by a crystal leave it in almost every direction, and the scattered waves cancel one another out except along a few sharp beams. <u>W. L. Bragg showed that such a beam appears only where the extra distance travelled by a wave turned back from one plane of atoms, rather than from the plane above it, comes to a whole number of wavelengths.</u> The relation contains the wavelength, the angle at which the beam leaves and the spacing between the planes. Two of the three can be measured directly, and the spacing follows.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It states the condition that makes the measurement described at the end of the text possible.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It explains why X-rays are scattered by the electrons of an atom at all.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It questions whether the sharp beams can be located accurately enough to be useful.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It describes the apparatus with which the scattered beams are recorded.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A hammered coin has an irregular edge, and a sliver pared from it leaves nothing behind to show what has been taken. Clipping was accordingly common, and was punished savagely without becoming rare. The screw press introduced in the seventeenth century struck coins of even shape and allowed a legend or a pattern of grooves to be impressed around the rim. A clipped coin now announced itself: the missing grooves could be seen across a counter, and the coin would not pass at its face value.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Machine striking discouraged clipping by making interference with a coin's edge obvious to anyone handling it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Clipping came to be punished more severely after the screw press was introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Hammered coins were struck less accurately than coins made by machine.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The screw press allowed mints to produce coins in far greater numbers than before.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Ethylene is a gas, and a ripening apple gives it off. The gas spreads through the air of a closed store and is taken up by the fruit around it, where it begins the same softening and the same conversion of starch to sugar that produced it. A single over-ripe apple will therefore bring a whole crate forward by several days. Commercial stores hold fruit in air from which the gas is continuously scrubbed, and bring a consignment on by admitting ethylene deliberately when the market calls for ripe fruit.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Commercial fruit stores keep their crops in air from which gases have been removed.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Because the ripening signal travels as a gas between fruit, ripening can be both spread by one fruit and controlled by a store.

choices.label: C
choices.content: An over-ripe apple gives off more ethylene than a fruit picked before it is ready.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Ethylene converts the starch held in a fruit into sugar and softens its flesh.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tveit's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Forecast accuracy at five days improved steadily from the 1980s onward, and two things changed across the same period: the models were run on far finer grids, and satellites began to supply temperature and humidity through the depth of the atmosphere over the oceans, where almost no measurements had existed. Meteorologist Ola Tveit argues that the improvement is owed chiefly to the new observations rather than to the finer grids.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Satellites now supply the great majority of the observations that enter a global forecast model.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Forecasts issued for two days ahead improved less across the period than forecasts issued for five days ahead.

choices.label: C
choices.content: When the modern model was rerun at its finest grid using only the observations available in 1980, its five-day forecasts were no better than those actually issued in 1980, while the 1980 model rerun with modern satellite data improved sharply.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The finest grids in use today divide the atmosphere into cells about a tenth the width of those used in 1980.

questions.stem: Which quotation from the log most effectively illustrates Falcó's claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An assistant at a hilltop observatory kept the nightly log for eleven years, recording the instrument used, the objects observed and the state of the air. Historian Nuria Falcó argues that the log is best read as a record of the atmosphere, into which the observing programme is entered only as whatever the air happened to permit on a given night.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.content: “Observations of the fourth satellite continued, and the times of the eclipses entered in the usual register.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “A visitor from the county society was shown the instrument between eleven and midnight.”

Emulsion chemist Karin Løvold argues that the speed of a plate is bought at the cost of the detail it can record.

questions.stem: A rain gauge at a weather station was not emptied overnight. Rain then fell at a steady rate all morning: the gauge held 7 millimetres of water at 11 in the morning and 16 millimetres at 2 in the afternoon. Which equation gives the depth d, in millimetres, of water in the gauge h hours after 9 in the morning?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A saddler's stitching horse will hold a strap no more than 210 centimetres long. Every strap is cut 18 centimetres longer than 4 times the length of the billet that will be sewn to it. What is the greatest possible length, in centimetres, of a billet whose strap the stitching horse will hold?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A cartwright's yard holds 3 times as many cart wheels as dray wheels. After 24 cart wheels are sold and 6 dray wheels are bought, the yard holds twice as many cart wheels as dray wheels. How many dray wheels did the yard hold at the start?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Bales were carried out of a mown field at a steady rate. Three hours after the loading began 264 bales were still in the field, and seven hours after it began 148 were still in the field. How many bales were in the field when the loading began?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The air in a tobacco curing barn warms at a constant rate once the flues are lit. Two hours after lighting a thermometer in the barn read 46 degrees Celsius, and five hours after lighting it read 64 degrees Celsius. The leaf is taken down when the thermometer reads 100 degrees Celsius. How many hours after lighting is the leaf taken down?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A seed cleaner passes a batch only if it carries at most 4 grams of chaff for each kilogram of seed. A batch of 45 kilograms of seed carries 294 grams of chaff, and each further run through the cleaner takes out 36 grams of chaff. What is the least number of further runs that will bring the batch within the limit?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A vineyard estimates the trellis wire needed for n rows, in metres, as \((3n+4)^{2}-\left(9n^{2}+7\right)\). Which expression is equivalent to this estimate?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The number of frost-free days in a year at a weather station is modelled by \(F(a)=180-\frac{a^{2}}{500}\), where a is the station's height above sea level in metres and \(0<a<300\). At what height, in metres, does this model give 135 frost-free days?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The area of leaf on a young vine, in square centimetres, is modelled by \(A(w)=24(1.5)^{w}\), where w is the number of weeks since bud break. According to this model, by what percent does the leaf area grow over any two-week stretch?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The volume of must a vineyard's press yields in one pressing varies directly with the square of the diameter of the press's ram. A press whose ram is 30 centimetres across yields 45 litres in a pressing. How many litres does a press whose ram is 40 centimetres across yield in a pressing?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A wheelwright sets the dish of a wheel by the rule \(D=\frac{r(s-2)}{4}\), where r is the rim radius, s is the number of spokes and D is the dish. Which expression gives s in terms of D and r?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The ripeness of a vineyard's grapes, measured in degrees Brix, is modelled by \(S(d)=d^{2}-4d+15\), where d counts the days after veraison and \(0\le d\le 30\). At what value of d does this model reach 75 degrees Brix?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A vineyard pays its pickers $4 for each lug box filled, and a full lug box holds 9 kilograms of grapes. How many dollars is a picker paid for a day on which that picker brings in 738 kilograms of grapes?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: After 12 percent of the leaf hung in a tobacco curing barn was thrown out as trash, 2,024 kilograms were left. How many kilograms of leaf were hung in the barn?
questions.subject: MATH

CropPassedFailed
Clover10020

Timothy7030

questions.stem: In one vineyard 14 rows gave a mean of 205 kilograms of grapes each, and 6 further rows gave a mean of 240 kilograms each. What was the mean yield, in kilograms, of these 20 rows?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A harness maker cuts a triangular gusset with two sides of equal length and a third side that is 7 centimetres shorter than each of the equal sides. The three sides together measure 71 centimetres. What is the length, in centimetres, of the shortest side of the gusset?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A vineyard row runs straight up a slope, rising 25 metres over a horizontal run of 60 metres. What is the value of the sine of the angle at which the row meets the horizontal?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rain gauge catches rain in a funnel whose circular mouth is 20 centimetres across, and every drop that lands in the funnel runs down into a cylindrical measuring tube 4 centimetres across. After a shower in which 1.2 centimetres of rain fell, how many centimetres deep does the water stand in the measuring tube?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A hay rick is built as a rectangular block 9 metres long, 5 metres wide and 4 metres high, carrying on top of it a prism whose triangular cross-section is 5 metres wide at its base and 2 metres tall. What is the total volume of the rick, in cubic metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: An observatory's dome shutter is opened by turning a crank. The number of turns t needed satisfies 6t+14=92. What is the value of t?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A silk reeler winds 45 grams of raw silk onto each skein. How many grams of raw silk are wound onto 16 skeins?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A carriage spring stands 260 millimetres high when nothing rests on it, and it settles 3 millimetres lower for each sack loaded onto it. Which expression gives the height of the spring, in millimetres, once s sacks have been loaded?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A carriage spring's deflection is modelled in the xy-plane by the line y=7x+4. This line crosses the y-axis at the point (0, k). What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A lens polisher's speed setting x satisfies \(3x-8>16\). Which of the following could be the value of x?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A spring maker's stock of 320 steel strips falls by 24 strips each day. After how many days are 152 strips left?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rack in a silk-reeling shed holds at most 24 skeins, and 9 skeins are on it already. What is the greatest number of further skeins that can be put on the rack?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A silk mill writes its cost estimate as \(4(3k+5)-7k\), where k is the number of reels running. Which expression is equivalent to this estimate?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The area of a telescope maker's baffle, in square centimetres, is \(x^{2}+9x+20\). Which expression is equivalent to this area?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A silk-reeling machine's thread tension is modelled by \(f(x)=-(x-4)^{2}+29\). What is the greatest value this model can take?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: An optician writes a magnification ratio as \(\frac{x^{9}}{x^{4}}\), where \(x>0\). Which expression is equivalent to this ratio?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A silk reeler reels 6 skeins in an hour. Working at this rate, how many hours does the reeler take to reel 78 skeins?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: When raw silk is reeled, the ratio of the mass of reeled silk to the mass of waste is 5 to 2. How many kilograms of waste are produced alongside 140 kilograms of reeled silk?

questions.stem: A rearing tray holds 45 cocoons, and 18 of them are double cocoons. One of the 45 cocoons is picked at random. What is the probability that it is a double cocoon? Give the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: In the xy-plane the midpoint of the segment joining the points (2, -5) and (10, 1) is the point (a, b). What is the value of a+b?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: An observatory pier is finished with a stone cap in the shape of a pyramid whose square base is 12 centimetres on a side and whose height is 10 centimetres. What is the volume of the cap, in cubic centimetres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A plate-drying rack rests on a solid block in the shape of a prism 40 centimetres long whose cross-section is a right triangle with legs of 8 centimetres and 15 centimetres. What is the volume of the block, in cubic centimetres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A mounting bracket is a right triangle ABC with its right angle at C. In this bracket \(\tan A=\frac{3}{4}\) and AC=24 centimetres. What is the length of BC, in centimetres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem:
A darkroom mixes a developer from x litres of one stock solution and y litres of another, and the mixture must satisfy both of the following conditions.
2x+5y=31
4x-3y=23
What is the value of \(\frac{x}{y}\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The two setting circles of a telescope mounting are drawn in the xy-plane as perpendicular lines. One of them is the line \(4x-6y=15\); the other passes through the point \((8,-1)\). What is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of the second line?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A spectacle grinder's setting x must satisfy both \(7x-4>3x+16\) and \(2x+5\le 41\). How many integer values of x satisfy both conditions?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A darkroom's stop bath is made up of 3 parts water to 1 part acid by volume. How many litres of water must be stirred into 8 litres of this stop bath so that the result is 5 parts water to 1 part acid?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A telescope drive's setting error is a linear function f for which \(f(3)=-2\) and \(f(9)=16\). For what value of x does \(f(x)=40\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A darkroom thermometer's tolerance is described by \(\left|2x-9\right|=13\). What is the sum of the values of x that satisfy this equation?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A darkroom worker has 240 minutes of bench time. Each contact sheet takes 6 minutes to print and each enlargement takes 14 minutes, and the worker must print at least 12 enlargements. What is the greatest number of contact sheets the worker can print in the 240 minutes?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A darkroom's dilution rule is the function f defined by \(f(x)=\frac{60}{x+3}\). For some number a it happens that \(f(a)=5\). What is the value of \(f(a-6)\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A spectacle grinder writes \(\frac{4x^{2}+5x-9}{x+2}\) in the form \(4x-3+\frac{k}{x+2}\), where k is a constant and \(x\ne -2\). What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A telescope maker's focal relation is \(\frac{18}{x}+x=11\), an equation with two solutions. What is the greater of the two solutions?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A silk mill's throwing ratio satisfies \(\frac{8^{x}}{4^{x-3}}=32\). What is the value of x?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The two leaf thicknesses a and b of a carriage spring satisfy \(\frac{a}{b}=\frac{5}{3}\). What is the value of \(\frac{2a+b}{b}\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: An observatory dome's profile is modelled by \(f(x)=x^{2}-8x+21\). Exactly one value of x other than 2 gives \(f(x)=f(2)\). What is that value of x?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A list of 8 exposure times has a mean of 34 seconds. Two further exposure times are added to the list, and the mean of the 10 times is 39.2 seconds. One of the two times added is 58 seconds. What is the other, in seconds?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A silk mill's output was 5,000 kilograms in its first year. The output rose by 6 percent in the second year and then fell by 6 percent in the third. What was the output, in kilograms, in the third year?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A contact printer works at a steady rate, turning out 200 prints in 3 hours and 20 minutes. At this rate, how many prints does it turn out in 5 hours and 15 minutes?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A drawer holds 40 photographic plates, of which 15 have not been exposed. Three of the unexposed plates are taken out of the drawer. If one of the plates still in the drawer is then chosen at random, what is the probability that it has not been exposed?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A telescope's finder bracket is a right triangle whose vertices sit at the points A(-3, 2), B(5, 2) and C(5, 8) of the xy-plane, with the right angle at B. The point M is the midpoint of side AC. What is the length of the segment BM?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: An observatory dome is a hemisphere whose curved surface area is \(72\pi\) square metres. What is the volume of this hemisphere, in cubic metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A telescope's tube ring is cut as right triangle ABC, whose right angle is at B. In this ring \(\cos A=\frac{7}{25}\). What is the value of \(\sin C\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A darkroom tank is a rectangular box with a square base and a height of 30 centimetres, and it holds 12,000 cubic centimetres. The inside of the base and the insides of the four walls are lined with felt. How many square centimetres of felt does the lining take?
questions.subject: MATH
